column1: # Every place the manuals contradict each other or the hardware, what we do about it,
# and the one experiment that would settle it. `aslmp ambiguities` prints this table.
# This is the file to hand a Mitsubishi application engineer. It is not a list of
# things we have not got round to; it is the list of decisions somebody had to make on
# incomplete evidence, with the evidence attached.
# readings   the mutually exclusive answers, '|' separated, at least two.
# chosen     what this library actually DOES. Sometimes that is neither reading but
#            "refuse", which is the right answer when guessing wrong would move a
# A resolved_by_measurement row carries the CPU and firmware in the provenance tail.
# It is resolved for THAT silicon and that firmware, and for nothing else: everything
# we know about PLC pathology is n=1.

column2: question
column3: readings
column4: chosen
column5: reason
column6: probe

column2: In a bit-unit Write Random with the long device specification, is ON written as the bytes 01 00 or as the little-endian encoding of 0x0100?
column3: 01 00 -- value 1, consistent with the ASCII rendering '0001' and with pymcprotocol|00 01 -- if the manual's '0100H' is a 16-bit value to pack little-endian
column4: 01 00. Only reachable with subcommand 0003, which an iQ-F refuses, so nothing we can test emits it today.
column5: The ASCII form is unambiguous and the binary form should encode the same value; reading 0100H as a literal byte pair is the only interpretation consistent with it.
column6: iQ-R only: write a known bit with each byte order and read it back.

column2: Is the subcommand for 1617 Clear Error 0000 or 0001?
column3: 0000 -- the FX5 detail section|0001 -- the FX5 command-list table on the same manual
column4: 0000, validated client-side; anything else raises.
column5: The FX5 manual's command-list table and its own detail section disagree. 0000 matches every other non-device command in the catalogue.
column6: Send 1617 with subcommand 0000 against a CPU with a clearable error and record the end code; repeat with 0001. Untested by us.
column14: 4.1 Command list (p.57-63) against the 1617 detail section

column2: Are the two bytes after the 4E serial number free for the client to use?
column3: Fixed value -- SH(NA)-080956ENG-M calls them a fixed value|Free -- SH(NA)-080008-AB's naming suggested 16 spare bits of correlation
column4: Send 00 00. Do not validate them on receive. Do not build anything on them.
column5: A request carrying AA 55 there came back with those bytes ZEROED -- not echoed, and not rejected. So they are not extra correlation bits, and a design that used them for a client-side transaction tag would silently lose it.
column6: Settled for FX5U.

column2: Does a PLC configured for ASCII accept lower-case hexadecimal digits and lower-case device mnemonics?
column3: Accepted -- nothing in the manuals says it is rejected|Rejected -- the manuals say to use capitalised codes
column4: Emit upper case always; refuse lower case on parse rather than normalising it silently.
column5: The manuals say 'use capitalized code' and never say what happens otherwise. Silently upper-casing a caller's input is the class of quiet fix-up this library refuses to do, and refusing costs nothing because we emit upper case.
column6: Needs a connection entry configured for ASCII, which the bench does not have: Communication Data Code is one Own Node setting for the whole FX5 Ethernet port, so switching it breaks every binary connection at once. Then send a 0401 with a lower-case device code and lower-case hex and record the answer.

column2: How do the ASCII fields of a device-memory-extension (subcommand 008x) request line up with the binary ones?
column3: As the manual's ASCII diagram draws them|As the manual's worked ASCII example reads
column4: Not implemented. The extension subcommand is out of scope for v1 in ASCII.
column5: The manual's 20-character ASCII block does not obviously correspond to the 11-byte binary block, and the diagram and the worked example do not settle it between them. Binary is unambiguous and verified.
column6: Capture a real ASCII extension request from GX Works3 or a third-party master, or get a byte-level example from MEAU.

column2: How many bit points fit in one binary 0401 Device Read (Batch) on an iQ-F?
column3: 7168 -- SH(NA)-080956ENG-M's generic/iQ-R figure|3584 -- JY997D56001-K's FX5 CPU module column|1792 -- the FX5 ASCII figure, sometimes quoted as if it were the binary one
column4: 3584 for every iQ-F profile in binary, 1792 in ASCII; 7168 for iQ-R.
column5: Binary-searched on the CPU: 3584 points from M0 returned 0x0000 and 3585 returned 0xC051. The manual that is family-specific wins over the generic one, and here the hardware agrees with it. A library that ships SLMP-REF's 7168 builds frames this CPU rejects.
column6: Already settled for FX5U. Repeat the binary search on an iQ-R to confirm 7168 there; it has never been tested.

column2: Which end code does an FX5 return for a device code it does not have or does not recognise?
column3: 0xC05B -- 'the module cannot read/write from/to the specified device', which is what the doc-derived mapping predicted|0xC05C -- 'error in request contents' -- observed
column4: 0xC05C. Its likely_cause leads with 'a device family this CPU does not have', and the client's own device table refuses V, ZR, DX and DY on iQ-F before the frame is built so a user should never see it for that reason.
column5: Device code 0x00, device code 0xFF, V0, ZR0 and DX0 all returned 0xC05C on the bench. 0xC05C is nominally a request-content code, so without this correction the library would tell a user their subcommand was wrong when their CPU simply has no edge relays.
column6: Settled for FX5U. An iQ-R may well return 0xC05B as documented; the row carries both.

column2: Which end code does a request-data-length mismatch produce, and what happens when the length is overstated?
column3: 0xC057 -- 'the request data length does not match the number of data in the character section', which the doc-derived mapping chose|0xC061 when understated, and NO RESPONSE AT ALL when overstated -- observed
column4: 0xC061. The asymmetry is ranked first in SlmpTimeoutError.likely_causes whenever a timeout arrives after PARTIAL bytes.
column5: Declaring L two bytes short returned 0xC061 and the connection recovered; declaring L as 0x0000 returned 0xC061 echoing command 0x0000 subcommand 0x0000; declaring L two bytes long produced no response at all and a 3000 ms timeout, because the CPU blocks waiting for bytes that never arrive. A client whose length arithmetic is wrong in one direction fails loudly and in the other looks exactly like a dead PLC. That asymmetry is why L is produced by exactly one expression in this package and guarded by three tests.
column6: Settled for FX5U.

column2: What does end code 0xCEE3 mean?
column3: An iQSS code alongside CEE0, CEE1 and CEE2|Not a documented code at all
column4: Not shipped as a row. It falls through to a generic SlmpEndCodeError with 'undocumented end code' and the report-it line.
column5: 0xCEE3 appears in none of SH(NA)-081257ENG-AD, SH(NA)-081105ENG-G or JY997D56001-K. It is in circulation in third-party code, which is not a source. A fabricated description in the error path is worse than an honest gap.
column6: Find it in a Mitsubishi manual, or leave it out.

column2: Which clear modes does 1001 Remote Run accept on an FX5?
column3: Only 00H -- JY997D56001-K p.105 clear-mode table has exactly one row|00H, 01H and 02H -- the communication example on the SAME page sets clear mode to 'clear all devices including that in the latch range' and prints 02H
column4: iQ-F profiles allow ClearMode.NONE only; anything else raises before the request is built.
column5: The FX5 manual contradicts itself on one page, and the consequence of guessing wrong is clearing a running machine's latch range. Refusing is the only defensible default when the document disagrees with itself and we have no measurement.
column6: 1001 with clear mode 01H and then 02H against a scratch program on a CPU in STOP: record the end code, and check whether devices actually cleared.

column2: How long after a client closes its TCP connection is the SLMP connection entry unavailable to the next connect to it?
column3: It is held for a fixed period after the close -- about 50 ms, diagnosed by an outside reviewer from a bench script that could not reconnect at all|It is not held for any period: the CPU releases the entry as it processes the FIN, so an immediate reconnect races that processing -- about 2 ms on our wired link, and invisible over Wi-Fi -- observed
column4: The second. Nothing in the library waits, retries or backs off: SlmpConnectionEntryBusyError still raises, and it now names both causes, the measured window and the settle that fixes the self-inflicted one. The benchmark scripts and `aslmp bench` take a named 5 ms settle (aslmp.tools.bench.ENTRY_RELEASE_SETTLE_S) before connecting to an entry they just released.
column5: Measured from argus-bench, wired, same /24, median RTT 3.64 ms, six trials per gap: a clean close() followed by a reconnect to the same entry succeeded 1/6 at a 0 ms gap, 2/6 at 1 ms, and 6/6 at 2 ms and at every gap up to 200 ms. From the laptop over Wi-Fi (median RTT ~7 ms) the same test was 30/30 at every gap including 0 ms, which is why the failure reproduces on wire and not on Wi-Fi: the link latency alone already exceeds the window. What has to elapse therefore tracks the LINK and not the clock, which is what racing the CPU's own FIN processing would look like from outside rather than a fixed hold period -- an inference from these timings, not something we can see inside the CPU, and a scan-cycle boundary would fit the same table. Either way the window is LINK-DEPENDENT, so a faster link is EXPECTED to widen it; that direction is a prediction and 3.64 ms is the fastest link we have. 2 ms is what this CPU did on this link from this host on this day, not a guarantee and not a spec value. Note the two rows also differ by HOST, not only by link, so a same-host wired-and-wireless pair is the experiment that would isolate latency and it has not been run. Teardown shape was NOT distinguished: close(), shutdown(RDWR) then close(), and an abrupt RST via SO_LINGER 0 all reconnected cleanly, but that comparison ran over Wi-Fi, where a clean close() at a 0 ms gap already succeeds 30/30 -- on that link nothing could have failed, so it rules nothing out and wants repeating on wire. The one teardown that did fail intermittently was a socket dropped without close() and left to the garbage collector.
column6: Settled for FX5U on this link, and only for this link. Repeat it on a faster one -- a gigabit switch at sub-1 ms RTT, or a client on the CPU's own segment -- where the window should be WIDER, and record the smallest gap that is clean 6/6 there. A single trial proves nothing: at a 1 ms gap this CPU succeeded twice in six. Two other things are unmeasured: repeat the teardown-shape comparison ON WIRE, where it could actually fail, and run the wired/wireless pair from ONE host so link latency is the only variable that moved.
column15: This is the correction to the 'the slot was free again immediately after it closed' sentence in A-ONE-TCP-CONNECTION: free to the CPU, not yet free to a client that asks within about 2 ms. It is also why an outside reviewer could not run bench/transports.py at all -- the raw-socket control released the entry and the client connected microseconds later. A 300 ms settle would work and would be 150x more than the measurement supports.

column2: Is the FX5 module-access extension specifier F8H or F9H?
column3: F8H -- SH(NA)-080956ENG-M for U[n]\G|F9H -- the FX5 appendix
column4: Unresolved; the extension subcommand (0x0080) is not implemented, so nothing in the library emits either byte.
column5: It only matters for buffer-memory access on FX5, which is out of scope for v1. Shipping a guess would put an unverifiable byte on the wire for no benefit.
column6: 0401 with subcommand 0080 against U0\G0 with each code; exactly one should answer.

column2: Which FX5S models do the codes 4B55H-4B58H identify?
column3: FX5S-30/40/60MT/ES and FX5S-80MT/ES|FX5S-30/40/60MT/ES and FX5S-80MT/ESS, as the survey extract of p.110 reads
column4: The first: 4B58H is recorded as FX5S-80MT/ES. The codes are the manual's; the model NAMES for these four rows are ours.
column5: The second reading cannot be right, because 4B5CH-4B5FH are already the 30/40/60/80 MT/ESS block, so 4B58H cannot also be 80MT/ESS. The four rows are shipped with provenance=inferred rather than dropped, because dropping them would make a real FX5S fail to identify.
column6: Re-read JY997D56001-K p.110 from a rendered page image, or run `aslmp identify` against an FX5S and compare.

column2: Does the FX5 built-in Ethernet port accept 4E frames on a connection entry configured as 3E?
column3: No -- JY997D56001-K 2.1 lists applicable frames as 3E and 1E only|No -- JY997D56201-B p.25 says communication is possible by SLMP 3E frames|Yes -- observed
column4: Default to 3E, permit 4E on iQ-F. The acceptance is labelled as observed on one CPU and one firmware, and is not contractual.
column5: A well-formed 4E binary 0401 returned a 4E response with serial 0x1234 echoed correctly as 34 12, on a connection explicitly configured 3E. Two Mitsubishi manuals say that is impossible. The CPU evidently dispatches on the subheader rather than on the entry's frame parameter. This matters more than it looks: 4E carries a serial, and the serial is the only in-band defence against the TCP coalescing corruption, which on 3E is undetectable.
column6: Ask MEAU whether the behaviour is intentional. If it is, defaulting to 4E on iQ-F would turn a silent wrong-data failure into a loud SlmpSerialMismatchError and is the largest correctness win still available.

column2: Are 0801 Monitor Registration and 0802 Execute Monitor usable on an iQ-F?
column3: No -- JY997D56001-K's command list does not list them for the FX5 CPU|No, and the refusal is 0xC059 rather than 0xC05D -- observed
column4: Capability-gated off on every iQ-F profile. monitor_register() raises SlmpCapabilityError citing the measurement, pre-transport. It is never emulated with a 0403 substitution.
column5: Both 0801 and 0802 returned 0xC059 (command or subcommand cannot be used by this CPU), measured twice through independent code paths. 0802 returning 0xC059 rather than 0xC05D is useful: there is no way to mistake it for 'you forgot to register'. Silently substituting a Read Random for a requested monitor would be exactly the kind of substitution this library refuses.
column6: Settled for FX5U. The positive iQ-R path -- registration lifetime, whether it is per connection or global, what two concurrent clients do -- has never been tested by anyone here.

column2: For an iQ-F, does the X/Y device-number field carry the linear index of the octal literal, or the octal digits reinterpreted as hexadecimal?
column3: Linear index -- Y45 goes on the wire as 0x25 (JY997D56001-K's 1E examples, written fresh for FX5 in rev G, and the device-table footnote)|Octal digits as hex -- Y27 goes on the wire as 0x27 (JY997D56001-K's 3E binary examples on p.79 and p.86)
column4: Linear index. parse_address treats X and Y as base 8 on iQ-F and transmits the integer value.
column5: Measured directly: writing a single bit at wire number 0, 8 and 16 lit linear output positions 0, 8 and 16. So GX Works3 Y20 (the 17th output) is 16 on the wire. The rev K 3E binary examples are traceable to un-recomputed copy-paste: rev D/E of the same manual prints the identical byte strings under Q-series hexadecimal captions (Y2F, X2F, Y17F). Those examples are excluded from the golden-vector corpus, with the exclusion recorded as data rather than as silence.
column6: Settled. The original probe was: force a known pattern on physical outputs, batch-read 16 bits from head 0 with device code 0x9D, and see which linear position moved.

column2: What do the individual iQ-R end codes in the 0x4000-0x4FFF block mean?
column3: The same as the FX5 codes of the same value, per JY997D55401 Appendix 3|iQ-R specific, per SH(NA)-081264ENG, which we have not read
column4: The FX5 meanings are shipped for the codes JY997D55401 documents. Any 0x4000-0x4FFF code not in the table raises SlmpCpuError with 'undocumented end code', the code formatted 0x%04X, and a request to report it with the CPU model and firmware.
column5: SH(NA)-081264ENG was never obtained. Inventing iQ-R meanings from the FX5 manual would be exactly the sort of plausible-looking fabrication the citation rule exists to prevent.
column6: Source SH(NA)-081264ENG (MELSEC iQ-R CPU Module User's Manual (Application)) and add the rows.
column14: Appendix 3, Error codes of the CPU module (4000H to 4FFFH) (p.593)

column2: In the 2-byte (subcommand 0002/0003) binary device code, which byte goes first?
column3: 9C 00 for X -- SH(NA)-080956ENG-M p.35/38 and SH(NA)-080008-AB p.68 write the code as 009CH|00 9C for X -- JY997D56001-K p.36/66 writes it as 9C00H and draws the wire that way
column4: 9C 00, per SH(NA)-080956ENG. Moot on iQ-F, which refuses subcommand 0002 outright.
column5: Exactly reversed between two Mitsubishi documents. pymcprotocol 0.3.0 implements 9C 00 and is reported working against iQ-R. JY997D56001-K contains no worked byte-level example using the long format anywhere, so its figure cannot be cross-checked inside its own manual.
column6: iQ-R only: send 0401 subcommand 0002 for D0 with device code bytes 9C 00, then with 00 9C. Exactly one should return 0x0000. Our FX5U cannot answer this -- subcommand 0002 returned 0xC059.

column2: Does 0619 Self Test really reject loopback data outside '0'-'9' and 'A'-'F'?
column3: Enforced -- both manuals restrict loopback data to those characters|Not enforced -- the CPU echoes whatever it is given
column4: Codec.loopback_payload_ok refuses non-hex payloads client-side, including our own defaults. The connect handshake sends b'0619' plus four hex digits of a per-generation nonce; self_test() defaults to b'ABCD'.
column5: b'ABCD' (41 42 43 44) is the exact payload proven on the bench, so the default is a measured value rather than a guess. Whether the restriction is enforced is unknown, and shipping a default that violates a documented constraint would be indefensible either way.
column6: Send 0619 with b'ZZZZ' and record whether it echoes, errors, or is silent.

column2: Does the FX5 CPU built-in port honour, ignore or reject a non-zero monitoring timer?
column3: Rejected or required to be 0000H -- JY997D56001-K p.27 says to specify 0000H for the CPU module|Accepted and inert -- observed
column4: MonitoringTimer.INDEFINITE (0x0000) is the default. Non-zero values are allowed and never imply the client-side deadline.
column5: 0x0000, 0x0010, 0x0028 and 0x00F0 all returned 0x0000 with correct data and statistically indistinguishable latency (p50 6.99 ms vs 7.14 ms over 200 transactions each). The field is neither rejected nor honoured in any way we can observe from outside.
column6: Settled for FX5U. On an Ethernet module the timer is documented to do something; untested.

column2: What happens to a second TCP connection to the same SLMP connection entry?
column3: It is refused at the TCP layer|The TCP handshake SUCCEEDS and the CPU then immediately sends a FIN, leaving the incumbent undisturbed -- observed
column4: A zero-byte read on the first read of a generation raises SlmpConnectionEntryBusyError, and connect() additionally does a non-blocking EOF check before sending a byte. Connection pooling is not offered.
column5: connect() on a second socket returned success in 5.4 ms, then recv() returned 0 bytes before anything was sent. The first connection kept working, and the slot was free again immediately after it closed. A client that treats 'connected' as 'ready' reports a healthy connection that dies on its first transaction, and one with reconnect logic spins.
column6: Settled for FX5U with this entry's connection count. The FX5U's eight-connection budget is shared across all SLMP, MELSOFT, socket and predefined-protocol entries, so the number is a configuration fact, not a CPU fact.

column2: What are the two fixed bytes after the subcommand in 1002 Remote Stop, 1005 Remote Latch Clear and 1006 Remote Reset?
column4: profile.remote_fixed_field: 00 00 on iQ-F, 01 00 on the SLMP-REF families. Never guessed, never retried in the other value.
column5: Both readings were confirmed from rendered page images, not from a text layer, so this is a genuine difference between two Mitsubishi documents rather than an extraction artefact. The family-specific manual wins for its own family. Historically (SH(NA)-080008) the field is a Mode fixed at 0001H, which is why 01 00 has evidently worked in the field on Q/L.
column6: FX5U in STOP with a scratch program: send 1002 with 01 00 and record the end code, then repeat with 00 00. We deliberately never sent any CPU-state command to the bench, so this is untested by us in both directions.
column14: 6.2/6.4/6.5 Remote Stop / Latch Clear / Reset (p.106-108); SH(NA)-080956ENG-M p.133/135/136 for the other reading.

column2: Which ASCII mnemonic and device code belong to the step relay S in each device specification format?
column3: S*/98H short and S***/0098H long -- SH(NA)-080008-AB p.68 and JY997D56001-K p.66|S**/98H and (S***)/(0098H) -- SH(NA)-080956ENG-M p.36 prints this row's two columns swapped relative to every other row
column4: S*/0x98 short, S***/0x0098 long, per SH(NA)-080008.
column5: Two of the three documents agree and follow the pattern every other row in the same table follows. The device code value 0x98 is not in doubt; only the ASCII padding is, and only in one document.
column6: Low priority. Send an ASCII 0401 for S0 with 'S*' and with 'S**' once an ASCII entry exists.

column2: What does an FX5 do when two SLMP messages arrive in one TCP segment?
column3: Both are processed, in order|Only the LAST is processed and the rest are discarded with no error -- observed
column4: At most one transaction in flight per TCP connection, enforced structurally by a single-use capability token rather than by convention. There is no public method anywhere in the package that puts bytes on a socket.
column5: Two 3E requests written back to back produced one response, and it answered the SECOND request. With 4E the serials made it unambiguous: three coalesced requests returned one response bearing the third serial, four returned the fourth. On 3E there is no correlation field at all, so the client pairs that response with the first request and a setpoint read returns a scan counter -- no error, no end code, no timeout, just wrong data, and the connection recovers afterwards so nothing alerts you. UDP does not have this failure, because datagrams are framed.
column6: Settled for FX5U.

column2: Will a PLC reject the device types the manual forbids in Read Random?
column3: Yes -- JY997D56001-K p.78 says TS, TC, STS, STC, CS and CC must not be used in Read Random and predicts CPU error 0x4032|No -- observed
column4: The client refuses TS, TC, STS, STC, CS, CC, LCS and LCC in random and monitor commands. We refuse what this PLC would have allowed.
column5: A 0403 with one word point at TS0 (device code 0xC1) returned end code 0x0000 and one word of data. The CPU accepted a request its own manual forbids. Any design that leans on the PLC to reject illegal requests inherits whatever that particular firmware happens to do.
column6: Settled for FX5U.

column2: How deep can requests be pipelined on a UDP connection entry before the CPU starts dropping them?
column3: Unbounded, since datagrams are independently framed|Clean to 32, roughly 31 percent lost at 64, with no error of any kind -- observed
column4: UDP pipelining is offered only with 4E serials, with a configurable and conservatively defaulted in-flight cap. A serial that never comes back raises. 3E over UDP is never pipelined.
column5: Bursts of 8 and 32 4E reads returned every response in order (363 txn/s at depth 32, against about 135 txn/s for serial TCP). A burst of 64 returned 44 of 64 with no end code, no ICMP and nothing else: the client only learns by timing out on a serial. Positional matching plus real loss equals silently mismatched replies, which is the TCP coalescing bug in a different costume.
column6: Settled for FX5U on one Wi-Fi link. The threshold is a property of the CPU's receive path and the network, and will differ elsewhere.

column2: Does an FX5 reject an X/Y literal containing the digits 8 or 9, which octal notation cannot express?
column3: The PLC rejects it, because Y8 is not an address the CPU has|The PLC accepts it and writes somewhere -- observed
column4: parse_address raises SlmpDeviceRadixError for any 8 or 9 in an X/Y literal on an iQ-F. The client is the only thing that will refuse it.
column5: Writing a bit at wire number 8 for Y returned end code 0x0000 and succeeded. Y8 and Y9 do not exist under octal notation. This is the second confirmed case of this CPU accepting a documented-illegal address, the first being a TS point in a Read Random, and together they are the reason client-side validation is treated as load-bearing rather than as a convenience.
column6: Settled.

column2: What does a request for ZERO device points return?
column3: An address error (0xC056), which is where the doc-derived mapping put it|0xC052, a word point-count error -- observed
column4: 0xC052. Commands validate a zero point count client-side and raise SlmpPointLimitError before sending.
column5: 0 word points from D0 returned 0xC052 on the bench. Zero points is a point-count problem, not an address problem, and the classification changes which exception subclass a caller catches.
column6: Settled for FX5U.

column2: Is the ZR file-register device number hexadecimal or decimal?
column3: Hexadecimal -- SH(NA)-080956ENG-M p.36 and SH(NA)-080008-AB p.68|Decimal -- JY997D56001-K p.67
column4: Hexadecimal, per SH(NA)-080956ENG.
column5: Moot on iQ-F, where ZR does not exist at all (ZR0 returned 0xC05C on our FX5U), so the FX5 manual is describing a device its own CPU does not have. Every third-party library we surveyed also treats ZR as hexadecimal.
column6: iQ-R only. Write known values to ZR0 and ZR16 from GX Works3, then read ZR16 over SLMP with device number 0x10 and with 0x16 and see which returns it.
